body:
Why did resistance develop?

British rule changed the ways land was owned, revenue was collected, forests were used and people were employed. These changes affected different communities in different ways. Tribal communities resisted the loss of customary rights over land and forests. Peasants protested against excessive rents, revenue demands, debt and forced cultivation. Industrial workers organised against low wages, long working hours and restrictions on their freedom.

These were not completely separate groups. A tribal cultivator could also be a tenant or a wage labourer. A peasant who lost access to land might migrate to a factory, mine or plantation. The main distinction is therefore the immediate grievance and the form of resistance, rather than an absolute division between communities.

Land revenue and changes in rural society

The East India Company became the Diwan of Bengal in 1765. As the chief revenue administrator, it sought income from agricultural land. Different revenue settlements subsequently determined who was responsible for paying the government and how the demand was assessed.

  • Permanent Settlement, 1793: Introduced in Bengal and adjoining areas, it recognised zamindars as revenue-paying intermediaries. The amount payable by the zamindar to the state was fixed permanently, but cultivators could still face high rents and insecure tenancy.
  • Ryotwari settlement: Introduced in important parts of southern and western British India, it assessed revenue directly on the individual cultivator, or ryot.
  • Mahalwari settlement: Introduced in parts of northern India, it assessed revenue on a village or revenue estate called a mahal. The village headman generally handled collection and payment.

The arrangements differed, but high demands, insecure rights and dependence on moneylenders could create hardship under more than one system. Land revenue was the payment demanded by the government; rent was generally the payment made by a tenant to a landlord. They should not be treated as identical.

Forest control and tribal livelihoods

Many tribal communities practised settled cultivation, shifting cultivation, hunting, gathering, herding or a combination of these activities. Shifting cultivation, also called jhum in some regions and podu in others, involved cultivating a forest plot for a period and then allowing it to recover.

Colonial forest administration restricted customary use of forests because the state wanted timber, revenue and greater control over land. The Indian Forest Act of 1865 established an important framework for state control. The legislation of 1878 distinguished reserved, protected and village forests. Restrictions were particularly severe in reserved forests. A later Indian Forest Act was enacted in 1927.

People who had relied on forest produce, grazing, hunting or shifting cultivation could lose access to these resources. Some were required to provide labour for the Forest Department or sought work elsewhere. Such changes contributed to tribal resistance.

Commercial agriculture and industrial employment

Colonial trade increased demand for crops such as indigo, cotton and tea. Commercial cultivation could create opportunities for some producers, but it could also expose cultivators to unstable prices, debt and coercive contracts. Indigo planters, for example, pressed peasants to cultivate a crop that many considered less profitable than food crops.

Factories and plantations created different forms of employment. Mill workers generally sold their labour for wages in industrial establishments, while many plantation workers lived under restrictive recruitment and employment arrangements. Their grievances increasingly led to strikes and collective organisations.

Diku was a term used by the Mundas and some neighbouring communities for outsiders associated with their exploitation. Begar means forced or unpaid labour. These terms help explain why tribal and peasant movements frequently opposed landlords, officials, contractors and moneylenders.

Prelims focus

  • 1765: The East India Company obtained the Diwani of Bengal.
  • 1793: Permanent Settlement recognised zamindars as revenue-paying intermediaries.
  • Ryotwari dealt directly with cultivators; mahalwari assessed a village or revenue estate.
  • The Indian Forest Acts of 1865, 1878 and 1927 are important colonial forest-law milestones.
  • Diku refers to an outsider; begar refers to forced or unpaid labour.
  • Trap: Tribal resistance, peasant resistance and labour movements can overlap in participants, even when their principal grievances differ.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, ch. 3, Ruling the Countryside, sections Revenue for the Company and A New System Is Devised; ch. 4, Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age, sections How Did Tribal Groups Live? and How Did Colonial Rule Affect Tribal Lives?; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–I, Class 9, 2018–19, ch. 4, Forest Society and Colonialism, sections Why Deforestation? and The Rise of Commercial Forestry.]

title: Colonial Rule and the Roots of Tribal, Peasant and Labour Resistance

body:
The Kol Uprising of 1831–32

The Kol Uprising took place in 1831–32 in the Chotanagpur region, much of which lies in present-day Jharkhand. It arose amid changes in landholding, revenue collection and local political authority.

Customary control over land was weakened when outsiders acquired rights over villages and cultivation. New landlords, contractors and moneylenders imposed demands that many local communities considered oppressive. The anger was directed not simply against one individual but against a wider system in which outsiders gained authority over land and its inhabitants.

The uprising included resistance by Kol and neighbouring tribal communities. Budhu Bhagat is associated with this period of resistance in Chotanagpur. British forces eventually suppressed the rebellion.

Santhal settlement in the Rajmahal Hills

The Santhals, also spelled Santals, were encouraged to settle and cultivate land near the Rajmahal Hills. In 1832, the colonial administration demarcated an area known as Damin-i-Koh for Santhal settlement.

The administration expected settled agriculture to expand cultivation and generate revenue. Santhal families cleared forests, established villages and cultivated fields. However, the growth of settlements also brought increasing involvement by moneylenders, traders, landlords and revenue officials.

When cultivators borrowed money, high interest and unfavourable transactions could leave them indebted. Land might be lost through debt or disputes. Santhals increasingly viewed the actions of moneylenders, landlords and officials as threats to the autonomy and livelihood they had expected from settlement.

The Santhal Hul of 1855–56

The Santhal Hul began in 1855 and continued into 1856. The word hul denotes an uprising or rebellion. The movement opposed oppressive moneylending, landlord demands and the colonial administration that sustained these arrangements.

The best-known leaders were the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu. Their brothers Chand and Bhairav, and the sisters Phulo and Jhano, are also remembered for their roles in the uprising.

The rebellion spread through Santhal areas and confronted representatives of colonial authority and local economic power. It was suppressed by British forces. The administration subsequently made separate arrangements for the Santhal Parganas, although this did not end all forms of exploitation.

How the 2 uprisings differ

Both movements arose in the broad Chotanagpur–Rajmahal region and involved opposition to outsiders who exercised power over land, revenue and credit. Their immediate historical settings were nevertheless different.

  • Kol Uprising: 1831–32; Chotanagpur; anger over land transfers, outsider authority and oppressive demands.
  • Santhal Hul: 1855–56; Rajmahal Hills and Damin-i-Koh; anger against moneylenders, landlords and colonial officials.

The Santhal Hul preceded the wider Revolt of 1857. It should be identified as a distinct tribal uprising rather than treated as a phase of the 1857 revolt.

Prelims focus

  • Kol Uprising: 1831–32, Chotanagpur.
  • Damin-i-Koh was demarcated for Santhal settlement in 1832.
  • Santhal Hul: 1855–56, Rajmahal Hills and surrounding Santhal areas.
  • Sidhu and Kanhu were prominent leaders of the Santhal Hul.
  • Chand, Bhairav, Phulo and Jhano are also associated with the Santhal uprising.
  • Trap: Birsa Munda did not lead the Santhal Hul; his movement belonged to a later period.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, ch. 4, Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age, section A Closer Look; NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part III, Class 12, ch. Colonialism and the Countryside, section The Santhals: Pioneer Settlers; Press Information Bureau, President of India Graces 9th International Santal Conference, 7 March 2026, and Prime Minister Pays Tribute to Brave Warriors on Hul Divas, 30 June 2026, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: The Kol Uprising and the Santhal Hul

body:
Birsa Munda and the Ulgulan, 1899–1900

Birsa Munda emerged as a major leader in the Chotanagpur region during the late nineteenth century. Born in 1875, he belonged to the Munda community. His followers regarded him as a spiritual leader, and he became widely known as Dharti Aba, meaning Father of the Earth.

The Mundas had customary systems of community landholding, including khuntkatti rights associated with the descendants of original village settlers. The growing influence of landlords, moneylenders, contractors and officials weakened customary control over land and increased demands for rent and labour.

Birsa's movement combined social and religious reform with political resistance. He urged followers to abandon liquor and certain practices he considered harmful, maintain village cleanliness and recover their dignity. At the same time, he opposed the exploitative power of dikus and the colonial government.

From 1895, Birsa called upon followers to restore an earlier, just social order. The political aim included the establishment of Munda Raj and the recovery of ancestral rights. He was arrested in 1895 and released in 1897. The major phase of the uprising, called the Ulgulan or Great Tumult, occurred in 1899–1900.

The movement was suppressed, and Birsa died in colonial custody on 9 June 1900. The Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, subsequently placed important restrictions on transfers of land, reflecting wider efforts to address tribal land alienation. It is a later legislative development, not an act enacted during the uprising itself.

The Bastar Rebellion of 1910

The Bastar Rebellion, also known as the Bhumkal Rebellion, took place in 1910 in the Bastar region of present-day Chhattisgarh. Forest reservation was a major cause.

In 1905, the colonial administration proposed reserving large areas of forest. Local communities feared losing access to forest produce, cultivation and customary livelihoods. Demands for unpaid labour and supplies further increased resentment.

The rebellion drew support from several communities. Gunda Dhur, associated with the Dhurwa community, is remembered as a prominent leader, although the movement did not have only 1 leader. British forces suppressed the rebellion but reduced the area proposed for reservation.

The Tana Bhagat movement

The Tana Bhagat movement began around 1914 among the Oraons of Chotanagpur. It is associated with Jatra Bhagat. The movement emphasised social and religious reform and opposed oppressive rent demands and forced labour.

Many Tana Bhagats later adopted Gandhian methods and participated in wider nationalist activity. This provides an example of a movement that began with local tribal grievances and subsequently developed connections with the national struggle.

The Rampa Rebellion of 1922–24

The Rampa Rebellion, also called the Manyam Rebellion, took place in the forested Agency areas of the Eastern Ghats in present-day Andhra Pradesh. Its leading figure was Alluri Sitarama Raju.

Forest restrictions, particularly those associated with the Madras Forest Act, 1882, interfered with shifting cultivation and customary access to forest resources. Local communities also protested against exploitation by police, revenue and forest officials, as well as demands for forced labour.

The uprising began in 1922 and continued until 1924. Raju mobilised hill communities against colonial authority. He was captured and killed on 7 May 1924. Unlike the non-violent methods associated with Gandhi, this rebellion used armed resistance, even though Raju also invoked ideas connected with the nationalist movement.

Do not confuse the forest-law contexts: Birsa Munda's movement centred strongly on customary land rights and outsider domination in Chotanagpur. Bastar's 1910 rebellion arose particularly from proposed forest reservation. The Rampa movement opposed forest restrictions and official oppression in the Andhra hill region.

Prelims focus

  • Birsa Munda: Chotanagpur; Ulgulan, 1899–1900; khuntkatti rights and Munda Raj.
  • Chotanagpur Tenancy Act: 1908, after Birsa's death.
  • Bastar or Bhumkal Rebellion: 1910; Gunda Dhur.
  • Tana Bhagat movement: around 1914; Jatra Bhagat and the Oraon community.
  • Rampa Rebellion: 1922–24; Alluri Sitarama Raju; Eastern Ghats.
  • Trap: Alluri Sitarama Raju belongs to the Andhra hill rebellion, not the Chotanagpur Ulgulan.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, ch. 4, Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age, section Birsa Munda; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–I, Class 9, 2018–19, ch. 4, Forest Society and Colonialism, section Rebellion in the Forest; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, ch. 2, Nationalism in India, section Rebellion in the Countryside; Press Information Bureau, Birsa Munda and Janjatiya Gaurav Divas explainer, November 2022, and Alluri Seetha Rama Raju: A Folk Hero of Rampa Rebellion, 9 August 2016, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Birsa Munda, Bastar and Rampa: Movements for Land and Forest Rights

body:
Bhil uprisings in Khandesh

The Bhils lived across the hill and forest regions of western and central India, including areas now in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. Their resistance cannot be reduced to 1 uprising under 1 leader.

In Khandesh, British occupation in 1818 was followed by repeated Bhil resistance. Uprisings occurred particularly during the period 1818–31. The extension of outside political control, interference with customary authority and economic hardship contributed to these conflicts.

The Bhil movements of Khandesh are geographically distinct from the later Naikda resistance in eastern Gujarat, although both arose in the broader western tribal belt.

Naikda resistance around Jambughoda

The Naikda movements took place in the forested areas around Jambughoda, in the historical Nárukot and Rewa Kantha region of present-day Gujarat.

During 1858–59, Naikda groups challenged British authority. Historical accounts describe attacks on colonial posts around Nárukot and Jambughoda. Some participants were connected with the wider disturbances associated with the Revolt of 1857.

Another important phase occurred in 1868. Joriya Parmeshwar, also called Joria Bhagat, and Rup Singh Nayak, or Rupsingh, mobilised followers in an effort to establish their own authority. The movement attacked government posts, including Jambughoda. British troops suppressed the uprising, and the principal leaders were subsequently captured and executed.

The 1868 movement combined opposition to colonial control with claims to local political and spiritual authority. Its leaders should not be confused with the Santhal or Munda leaders of eastern India.

Govind Guru and the Bhagat movement

Govind Guru, also known as Govindgiri, became an important reformer and organiser among Bhil communities of the Rajasthan–Gujarat border region. His Bhagat movement emphasised moral reform, social discipline and resistance to exploitative practices.

The movement also challenged burdens such as begar and oppressive demands by officials and local authorities. The issues therefore extended beyond religious or social reform to the conditions under which Bhil communities lived and worked.

The Mangarh tragedy, 17 November 1913

On 17 November 1913, Bhil followers associated with Govind Guru gathered at Mangarh Hill. The hill is located in present-day Banswara district, Rajasthan, close to Gujarat. British and allied princely-state forces fired on the gathering, killing many participants.

The event is remembered as the Mangarh massacre. It is significant to the history of tribal resistance in both Rajasthan and Gujarat because the communities and movement extended across the present-day state boundary.

Geographical distinction: Jambughoda is in present-day Gujarat; Mangarh Hill is in present-day Rajasthan near Gujarat. Their historical connections do not make them the same location.

Prelims focus

  • Bhil uprisings in Khandesh occurred after British occupation in 1818.
  • Naikda resistance around Jambughoda included the phases of 1858–59 and 1868.
  • Joriya Parmeshwar and Rup Singh Nayak are associated with the 1868 Naikda uprising.
  • Govind Guru is associated with the Bhil Bhagat movement.
  • Mangarh massacre: 17 November 1913, Mangarh Hill, present-day Rajasthan.
  • Trap: The Bhil and Naikda movements should not be merged into a single uprising with a single leader.

[Sources: IGNOU, History of India, 1707–1950, unit on Popular Resistance, section The Uprising of the Bhils, 1818–31; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Nárukot, History and Places of Interest, pp. 175 and 178; Press Information Bureau, PM Lays Foundation Stone and Dedicates Projects in Jambughoda, Gujarat, 1 November 2022; Press Information Bureau, Mangarh Dham ki Gaurav Gatha, 1 November 2022; online sources consulted 20 November 2026.]
